A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LEXam and provide readable main text, figures, tables and complete appendices. The retained material can be matched across formatting changes and renumbering.

before.justification: v6 reports original model evaluations, choice-count perturbation experiments and expert validation of LLM judges, including Tables 1–3 and Appendices C–I.

after.justification: v7 retains these experiments and adds a 16-choice model comparison and original human-performance findings in Appendix J.

M1.justification: The answering prompts, judging prompt and minimum-score ensemble of GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-32B remain unchanged. Varying distractor counts was already implemented in v6's perturbation study; its expanded evaluation does not introduce a new algorithm.

E1.justification: Sixteen-choice testing expands beyond v6's Swiss-only, five-statement perturbation subset to international-law material and four- or five-statement items in v7 Figure 5. Appendix J also examines human-written answers. The source exams, languages and overall legal domains remain.

E2.justification: v7 adds a 21-model MCQ-16 comparison, including GPT-5.2, Claude-4.6-Sonnet, Qwen3.5-plus, GLM-5, Kimi-k2.5 and MiniMax-m2.5. The retained MCQ-4 table replaces EuroLLM-9B-it with Apertus-8B, and Appendix J adds human comparators. The open-question and original seven-model perturbation comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported MCQ construction expands from 1,660 four-choice items plus a 385-item perturbation subset to 4,696 items with 4–32 choices. Section 4.2 shifts its primary evaluation to 16 choices. Appendix J introduces a 30-question, two-participant human test; the open-question split and expert-validation design remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 5 replaces four-choice subgroup diagnostics with MCQ-16 diagnostics, and Figure 4 revises open-question subgroup estimates. Appendix J adds an exploratory assessment of judge applicability to human answers. The existing choice-count robustness study and judge-bias, cross-language and failure-mode analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Bootstrapped standard errors, expert-agreement statistics, Alt-test procedures and multiple-testing correction remain unchanged. The new MCQ-16 table follows the existing uncertainty-reporting practice; the human study introduces no additional uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: New Table 9 reports MCQ-16 results, including GPT-5.2 at 52.53% and Claude-4.6-Sonnet at 52.43%; these are not same-setting improvements over v6's main four-choice comparison. Table 10 removes EuroLLM's 23.31% entry and adds Apertus-8B at 6.42%. Appendix J reports human accuracies of 60% and 80%. Figure 4's subgroup estimates change despite unchanged aggregate open-question tables.

T1.justification: The Alt-test definitions and mathematical testing procedure in Section 5.2 are retained. No new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs appear.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction revise the benchmark-size claim from 4,886 to 7,537 questions and emphasize variable-choice MCQs. The principal claims about challenging legal reasoning, process-based evaluation and expert-validated LLM judging remain unchanged.

C2.justification: New Appendix J limits direct human–model comparisons because of answer-distribution differences, time constraints, judge misalignment and students' specialized preparation. It also tentatively attributes the human MCQ results to legal expertise, while acknowledging the small sample. Existing limitations concerning language, jurisdiction and outdated legal material remain.

D1.justification: v7 removes v6 Tables 6–7, losing detailed MCQ composition by jurisdiction, language, course and year. It adds a future-leaderboard pointer and removes the opening GitHub/Hugging Face disclosure, while retaining the project page and general release statement. Prompts, inference settings, hardware and cost documentation remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 6.1 newly positions LEXam as complementary to task-specific legal benchmarks and explains why aligned comparisons would require substantial reformatting. References to newer evaluated models and Tian et al. (2026) are added; the broader related-work account and novelty positioning remain.

P1.justification: Most prose and section order are retained. Local revisions distinguish MCQ-4 from MCQ-16, move the four-choice results discussion into Appendix C.2, add acknowledgements and human-performance Appendix J, and relabel the existing future-plans appendix as K.

P2.justification: The document adopts ICLR formatting throughout, changing the title block, running headers, heading typography and text/float placement. Figure 1 is redrawn, Figures 4–5 are replotted and displayed in reversed order, and Figure 5 changes axes and statement-count legends. A separate MCQ-16 table is added and two MCQ-statistics tables are removed.

improvement.justification: v7 provides useful evidence about newer models on demanding MCQs and clarifies limits on grading human answers. However, it removes granular MCQ documentation, reports 7,537 questions while Table 4 retains 4,886, and suggests human superiority without publishing model scores for the same 30-question subset. These experimental gains and reporting weaknesses leave the net direction of overall quality unclear.
